::: {.callout-warning}
## Synthetic data
Everything numerical on this page is generated by a seeded random number generator inside the document. It is an exercise in publishing, not an observation of anything.
:::

## Why a standard error

A sample mean $\bar{x}$ varies from sample to sample, and the spread of its values is described by the standard error [@student1908]. For $n$ independent observations with standard deviation $\sigma$ it is given in @eq-se.

$$
\mathrm{SE}(\bar{x}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$ {#eq-se}

The mean of a long list is steadier than the mean of a short one, and @eq-se says by how much: four times as many observations halve the standard error.[^fn-halve]

[^fn-halve]: Because $\sqrt{4} = 2$. The rule assumes independent observations with a common $\sigma$.

## A synthetic experiment

The cell below draws samples of several sizes from one invented normal distribution, with a fixed seed, and measures the spread of their means. It uses only the Python standard library.

::: {#compute-means .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import math, random, statistics

SIZES = [4, 16, 64, 256]
REPEATS = 400
random.seed(20261114)

def sample_mean(n):
    return statistics.fmean(random.gauss(10.0, 2.0) for _ in range(n))

spread = {n: statistics.stdev(sample_mean(n) for _ in range(REPEATS)) for n in SIZES}
expected = {n: 2.0 / math.sqrt(n) for n in SIZES}
print({n: round(spread[n], 3) for n in SIZES})
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
{4: 1.053, 16: 0.484, 64: 0.241, 256: 0.127}
```
:::
:::


@fig-spread plots the measured spread against the value of @eq-se, and @tbl-spread lists both.

::: {#cell-fig-spread .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from IPython.display import SVG, display

W, H, left, bottom, top = 520, 260, 56, 220, 24
top_value = max(spread.values()) * 1.1
bars = []
for i, n in enumerate(SIZES):
    x = left + 28 + i * 112
    h = (bottom - top) * spread[n] / top_value
    e = (bottom - top) * expected[n] / top_value
    bars.append(
        f'<rect x="{x}" y="{bottom - h:.1f}" width="56" height="{h:.1f}" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.75"/>'
        f'<circle cx="{x + 28}" cy="{bottom - e:.1f}" r="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/>'
        f'<text x="{x + 28}" y="{bottom + 22}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="currentColor">n = {n}</text>'
    )
svg = (
    f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 {W} {H}" width="{W}" height="{H}" role="img">'
    f'<line x1="{left}" y1="{bottom}" x2="{W - 16}" y2="{bottom}" stroke="currentColor"/>'
    f'<line x1="{left}" y1="{top}" x2="{left}" y2="{bottom}" stroke="currentColor"/>'
    + "".join(bars) + "</svg>"
)
display(SVG(svg))
```

::: {#tbl-spread .cell tbl-cap='Measured spread and the formula\'s value, by sample size. Synthetic data.' execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

rows = ["| n | Measured spread | Formula, $\\sigma/\\sqrt{n}$ | Ratio |", "|---:|---:|---:|---:|"]
for n in SIZES:
    rows.append(f"| {n} | {spread[n]:.3f} | {expected[n]:.3f} | {spread[n] / expected[n]:.2f} |")
display(Markdown("\n".join(rows)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown}
| n | Measured spread | Formula, $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ | Ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 1.053 | 1.000 | 1.05 |
| 16 | 0.484 | 0.500 | 0.97 |
| 64 | 0.241 | 0.250 | 0.96 |
| 256 | 0.127 | 0.125 | 1.02 |
:::
:::


The ratios in @tbl-spread are close to one: with 400 repeats the measured spread agrees with the formula to a few percent, which is what the method of resampling relies on [@efron1993].

## What this shows, and what it does not

::: {.callout-note}
## What the test of this page is
That a document with seeded code can be executed on request, rendered without recomputing, and published through the site with its equations, figure, table, citations and notes intact. It does not show that the numbers above are right for any real data.
:::

Rerunning the computation gives the same figures, because the seed is fixed. A different seed would give slightly different ones, and they would still agree with @eq-se.
